Splitting $90,000 evenly across Amcor, UPS and Ford would generate about $5,000 a year in dividends, an average yield near 6%.

Three companies behind everyday packaging, parcel delivery, and pickup trucks all pay quarterly dividends. Had you put $30,000 into each of these three (a packaging maker, a parcel carrier, and an automaker), the $90,000 total would return about $5,067 a year in passive income.

RiverNorthPhotography / Getty Images

For retirees living off a portfolio, that cash shows up on a schedule, no matter what the market does. Here's what a $30,000 stake in each of these three high-yield names would return using each company's latest regular quarterly dividend, annualized at Nov. 13, 2026 prices, so they'll shift as prices and dividends change.

Ford Motor Turns Pickups Into a 5.03% Yield

Stock #3: Ford Motor (NYSE:F)

Yield (forward, regular dividend only): 5.03%

Shares for $30,000: 2,516.78

Annual Passive Income: ~$1,510

Ford makes gas and hybrid vehicles, sells work trucks and vans through Ford Pro, develops EVs in Model e, and loans to buyers through Ford Credit. The regular dividend has stayed at $0.15 every quarter in 2026, and the latest one is due Dec. 1. The larger payments in February 2024 ($0.33) and February 2025 ($0.30) aren't counted here.

The yield is high mostly because the stock trades at about 4 times free cash flow. In the third quarter, Ford returned $4.7 billion of adjusted free cash flow and ended the period with $25.3 billion in cash. It also reaffirmed full-year guidance of $6.0 billion to $7.0 billion. Uneven earnings remain the chief concern, as Ford posted a $1.327 billion second-quarter net loss after special charges, and management expects Model e to lose about $4 billion this year.

title: Lawyers could pocket up to $100M of Amazon's $309.5M refund settlement — claims are due by Dec. 1
detail:
Lawyers could pocket up to $100M of Amazon's $309.5M refund settlement — claims are due by Dec. 1
Becky Robertson
Sat, November 14, 2026 at 7:00 AM PST 4 min read
AMZN
Trade AMZN on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
shutterstock.com / flysnowfly

An ongoing class-action lawsuit against Amazon [NASDAQ: AMZN] is set to restore a whopping $309.5 million into the hands of U.S. shoppers, who claimed that some of the e-commerce juggernaut's return practices infringed upon federal consumer protection rights.

But the legal fees for the high-profile cases may end up commandeering nearly a third of the amount paid out, with counsel able to seek up to $100 million in compensation for its representation.

Must Read

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 5 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP

For some customers impacted, a claim form must be submitted before the upcoming Dec. 1, 2026 deadline. Here's what you need to know.

What does the case concern?

Complainants started filing with the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington back in 2023, alleging that Amazon had failed to properly honor its own chargeback policies in some cases.

The legal action asserts that, in contradiction to the "free, no hassle returns" that the $2.8 trillion company pledges, the brand "routinely … fails to issue refunds or re-charges customers who have returned items in compliance with its refund and exchange policies because of defects in [its] return and refund processes."

Plaintiffs also claim that "Amazon knows that most of its customers do not notice, and as a result, Amazon's practices result in substantial unjustified monetary losses by consumers."

A motion requesting preliminary approval of a settlement option proposed in January of this year was approved in August. This does not infer guilt or liability on Amazon's part, but is common in such proceedings to avoid what would inevitably be a long and costly trial. The amount is expected to be enough to cover all entitled purchases, plus interest.

The retail platform denies the allegations and any wrongdoing in the matter.

Read More: Vanguard reveals what's coming for U.S. stocks — and it could be bad news for this group of investors

Who is eligible for a settlement payout?

To qualify for the class action, you must have bought an item from Amazon.com and attempted a refund through its proprietary fulfillment channel, but either received no reimbursement at all, received the money back but were later charged for the returned product, received an untimely refund or received a refund of the wrong amount. The sale must have been made between Sept. 5, 2017 and Feb. 12, 2026.

title: Billionaire Bill Ackman Says There’s a Huge Disconnect in Wall Street’s Expectations for Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, and Alphabet
detail:
Billionaire Bill Ackman Says There’s a Huge Disconnect in Wall Street’s Expectations for Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, and Alphabet
Adam Levy, The Motley Fool
Sat, November 14, 2026 at 7:05 AM PST 5 min read
GOOGN
AMZN
MSFT
META
^GSPC
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The stock market hasn't been as keen on the hyperscalers in 2026 as it was in years past. Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) have delivered better returns than the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) year to date thanks to strong relative performances over the past month or so. Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL) and Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) haven't fared nearly as well — they're down for the year.

But that could be an opportunity for long-term retail investors. Billionaire hedge fund manager Bill Ackman believes the market has soured on these four stocks due to a "notable disconnect" between market expectations and the businesses' fundamentals. That's reflected in growing skepticism among analysts that the massive amounts these companies are spending on new data centers will yield meaningful returns on investment.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

But the actual financial results and management's commentary should give investors confidence that the future may be brighter for these hyperscalers than the average analyst expects.

Pershing Square CEO Bill Ackman. Image source: Getty Images.

The huge disconnect on Wall Street

In his third-quarter letter to Pershing Square shareholders, Ackman expressed his belief that most analysts aren't properly accounting for the potential revenue growth stemming from the stepped-up capital spending among Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, and Alphabet. He wrote:

Consensus analyst estimates for the hyperscalers reflect a notable disconnect: they expect the current level of capital intensity to persist for years into the future, yet they assume minimal acceleration in revenue growth beyond this year and next. Consensus estimates treat the capex buildout as a structural increase in maintenance capital intensity rather than as an investment capable of producing outsized future revenue growth and attractive returns on capital.

That is to say, Wall Street is acting like the increase in capital expenditures won't result in a commensurate increase in revenue over time. That's despite the fact that their prior spending has already been doing so for all four hyperscalers.

Meta, notably, saw accelerating growth in its advertising business as it accelerated its capital expenditures. And with the potential to grow its Muse agentic AI service, expand business messaging, and collect licensing revenue from its large language models (LLMs), it could see a sharp rise in direct artificial intelligence monetization in the near future.

title: MercadoLibre vs. Uber Technologies: Which Consumer Network Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

MercadoLibre vs. Uber Technologies: Which Consumer Network Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?
Brendan Coffey, The Motley Fool
Sat, November 14, 2026 at 7:32 AM PST 6 min read
UBER
MELI
AMZN
V
MA

Trading disclosure

Investors searching for high-growth platforms often find themselves choosing between regional dominance and global ubiquity. Whether MercadoLibre (NASDAQ:MELI) or Uber Technologies (NYSE:UBER) fits your portfolio better depends on your specific growth objectives.

MercadoLibre serves as the primary digital commerce infrastructure for Latin America, providing essential retail and fintech services. Uber connects millions of consumers with transportation and delivery options worldwide. While both operate platform-based models, they navigate different competitive landscapes and regulatory environments, making this a classic match-up for growth-oriented investors.

The case for MercadoLibre

MercadoLibre operates a vast digital ecosystem that includes its marketplace, the Mercado Pago fintech platform, and a comprehensive logistics network. The company maintains key partnerships with major media brands like Disney+ for its loyalty program and utilizes cloud infrastructure from Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN). It also works with card associations like Visa Inc. (NYSE:V) and Mastercard (NYSE:MA) to facilitate payment services for its millions of active users.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached about $38.5 billion, which represents a growth rate of approximately 47% over the prior year. The company reported net income of roughly $1.9 billion during this same period. This significant growth is a result of expanding electronic commerce adoption and the rising volume of digital payments throughout the region.

The debt-to-equity ratio, which measures total debt relative to shareholder equity, is nearly 1.7x. As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio of 1.2x indicates its ability to cover short-term liabilities with current assets. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was about $10.8 billion, providing capital to reinvest in the business among retail stocks.

The case for Uber Technologies

Uber Technologies connects over two hundred million monthly users with mobility and delivery services through its expansive global platform. The company has established significant partnerships with Tractor Supply Company (NASDAQ:TSCO) and Amazon to broaden its reach into grocery and retail delivery. It also relies on third-party mapping and infrastructure software from Alphabet to ensure its services run smoothly across thousands of cities.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, Uber recorded revenue of about $56.5 billion, an increase of roughly 14% compared to the previous twelve-month period. Net income for the company reached approximately $3.5 billion during this time. These results reflect the scale of the platform as it moves toward consistent profitability and stronger bottom-line performance.

Key Takeaways

BIT Capital's 13F for the quarter ended Sept. 30 shows it sold all of its Sandisk, Ciena and Nokia shares, while adding to Amazon and NVIDIA.

All three stocks it sold have fallen at least 39% since Sept. 30.

Analysts' average price targets sit 80% to 131% above the latest close for each of the three.

At about 4x forward earnings, Sandisk is the exit worth second-guessing, while Ciena's 27x makes that sale the easiest to defend.

A $2.8 billion fund just sold out of three of the AI build-out's big winners: Sandisk (SNDK:NASDAQ), Ciena (CIEN:NYSE) and Nokia (NOK).

BIT Capital's 13F for the quarter ended Sept. 30, filed Nov. 13, shows it held none of the three at quarter's end. That 13F holds $2.81 billion of US stocks across 93 positions. Over the same quarter, the fund added to Amazon (AMZN:NASDAQ) and NVIDIA (NVDA:NASDAQ), now its No. 2 and No. 3 holdings.

Sandisk was the biggest of the three

At June 30, BIT Capital held 85,743 Sandisk shares worth $195 million, 6.7% of its 13F stocks at the time. By Sept. 30, it held none. A 13F can't tell us when in the quarter the fund sold or what it got. But Sandisk is down 61% from its Sept. 30 close, including a 24% drop in a single week on industry-wide memory worries.

Analysts' average target has held close to its July high, and it's up from $137 a year ago:

Sandisk (SNDK): analysts' consensus (mean) price target, $ per share, last year (TIKR)

At $2,047, that target is more than double the latest close of $885.

Ciena got caught in the AI selloff

At June 30, the fund held 168,866 Ciena shares worth $83 million, 2.8% of its 13F stocks, and it held none by Sept. 30. Ciena is down 43% since then. That includes a 15% drop on Nov. 5 alongside Arista as the AI selloff deepened after the Democratic sweep.

Analysts' average target more than tripled over the past year to $513, and it has come down only a little from its June high of $566:

Ciena (CIEN): analysts' consensus (mean) price target, $ per share, last year (TIKR)

When Ciena reports in December, the question is whether its margins can keep up.

Nokia found a buyer on the other side

At June 30, the fund held 4.62 million Nokia shares worth $61 million, 2.1% of its 13F stocks, and none by Sept. 30. Nokia is down 39% since then. In its Oct. 22 third-quarter report, it beat expectations and held its outlook but cut its cash flow view, and the stock sank 9%. Not every fund headed for the exit: ARGA Investment Management's latest 13F shows it bought Nokia.

Key Takeaways

Scott Galloway expects Anthropic's Nov. 19 debut to open 15% to 40% above its IPO price.

A pop would lift Alphabet's and Amazon's stakes; earlier mark-ups more than tripled their second-quarter profits.

Investors look past those gains: Alphabet trades at 21x normalized forward earnings.

The bigger win is Anthropic funding its computing bills, including $121 billion committed to Google.

Alphabet (GOOG) and Amazon (AMZN:NASDAQ) are about to get a public price on a huge investment.

Anthropic will price its IPO on Nov. 18 and start trading as "ANT" the next day. Its amended S-1 sets a range of $70 to $78 a share, a fully diluted value of about $1.26 trillion to $1.40 trillion. Bloomberg reports it's multiple times oversubscribed.

NYU Stern professor Scott Galloway asked one of the deal's banks for as many shares as it can get him. On Pivot, he explained: "I don't know where the stock's going to be in a year. I'm fairly certain the first trade is 15 to 40% higher than the pricing."

Alphabet and Amazon Have Been Here Before

Each higher Anthropic round showed up in their net income as a gain. NewEdge Wealth's Cameron Dawson said on Bloomberg Surveillance that Anthropic and SpaceX gains "were massive drivers of earnings upside in 1Q and 2Q of 2026."

GOOG Quarterly Net Income: Q4 2024-Q3 2026 (TIKR)

Alphabet earned $112 billion in the second quarter, against $28.2 billion a year earlier. A $99.0 billion gain on equity securities made up $6.26 of its $9.11 of EPS. The third quarter went the other way: an $8.7 billion loss cut EPS by $0.55. Over nine months, Alphabet booked $127.3 billion of net equity gains, more than its $121.0 billion of operating income.

Amazon's second quarter included $53.4 billion of pre-tax other income, primarily from Anthropic, and net income more than tripled to $62.6 billion:

AMZN Quarterly Net Income: Q4 2024-Q3 2026 (TIKR)

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Alphabet, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Alphabet's Analyst Ratings

What a Pop Would Add

Anthropic's May funding round valued it at $965 billion. Dawson called a $1.1 trillion debut "an uplift to somebody like Google," but the range already starts higher. A 15% to 40% pop would put the first trade at roughly $1.45 trillion to $1.97 trillion, 50% to 104% above the May round.

Alphabet doesn't disclose its stake's size. It's also among the companies buying $26 billion of Anthropic stock at the IPO price in a private placement, so a pop marks those shares up on day one too.

In the news release, "Amazon workers in Delta win first union contract in North America", issued 13-Nov-2026 by Unifor over PR Newswire, we are advised by Unifor that changes have been made. The complete, updated release follows, with additional details at the end:

Amazon workers in Delta win first union contract in North America

VANCOUVER, BC, Nov. 13, 2026 /CNW/ -- 800 workers at Amazon's YVR2 fulfilment centre are now covered by a binding collective agreement after an independent arbitrator set its terms on Nov. 13, 2026. The agreement is the first for Amazon workers anywhere in North America and includes wage increases bringing hourly rates to $29 by the end of the agreement, enhanced severance protections of up to 18 weeks, and an additional week of vacation for workers with 10 years of service.

Smiling Amazon worker in a high-visibility vest holds a box beside a warehouse conveyor system.

"Amazon told everyone a union contract would never happen, but workers proved them wrong," said Unifor National President Lana Payne. "These workers stood up to one of the most powerful companies on earth and won rights in writing that Amazon cannot take away. Their courage won the day."

The B.C. Labour Relations Board certified Unifor Local 114 as the workers' union in July 2025 after finding Amazon hired extra staff to frustrate the workers' organizing drive and ran a "lengthy and pervasive anti-union campaign." On Aug. 4, 2026, the Board ordered binding arbitration, finding Amazon's conduct had affected the parties' ability to reach an agreement.

"Amazon tried to convince workers that they were too big to organize and used their power and money to deter workers while making billions in profits. They have fought every decision and tried to rewrite reality at every step but they have failed," said Western Regional Director Gavin McGarrigle. "These Amazon workers now have the binding union contract they deserve and we intend to support them and thousands more improving their lives, in BC and elsewhere."

Other gains in the three-year agreement include a Women's Advocate, a grocery benefit for the duration of the contract, statutory holiday scheduling based on seniority, and protections ensuring employee benefits remain equivalent to or better than existing coverage.

The agreement runs until November 13, 2029. Unifor will hold information sessions for YVR2 members in the coming days to explain their new rights and how to use them.

Workers at other Amazon sites in Metro Vancouver can talk to a Unifor organizer in confidence at organizing@unifor.org

Unifor is Canada's largest union in the private sector, representing 320,000 workers in every major area of the economy. The union advocates for all working people and their rights, fights for equality and social justice in Canada and abroad, and strives to create progressive change for a better future.

Update: The fourth paragraph has been amended to attribute the quote to Gavin McGarrigle. An earlier version of this release inadvertently omitted the attribution.

On Thursday, Fermi said the hyperscaler is advancing an initial 600 MW of power capacity beginning in 2027.

No definitive long-term lease has been signed; the customer is committing capital ahead of a lease to secure power within its targeted timeline, the company said.

Fermi said it plans to mobilize on site by December 1 and targets initial power in late second quarter or early third quarter of 2027.

Shares of Fermi Inc. (FRMI) extended their rebound on Friday, clocking their best day ever, and building on a sharp Thursday advance after the company disclosed major commitments from an unnamed investment-grade hyperscaler for 600 megawatts of power capacity at its Project Matador campus near Amarillo, Texas.

The Financial Times on Friday reported that people familiar with the matter identified the customer as Amazon, marking a reversal of earlier investment talks that collapsed last December. Amazon is expected to build its own data centers on the site, according to the people cited by the FT.

See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox

FRMI shares closed up 26% on Friday on the report.

Hyperscaler Commitments And Site Progress

Fermi is a pre-revenue developer of large-scale AI data-center campuses with dedicated on-site power. Co-founded in early 2025 by former U.S. Energy Secretary Rick Perry and energy financier Toby Neugebauer, it went public in October 2025 with a pitch for the world's largest such campus.

On Thursday, Fermi said an investment-grade hyperscaler is advancing an initial 600 MW of power capacity at Project Matador beginning in 2027. The customer has agreed to a $200 million prepayment, a $15 million early construction and site-development agreement, and the two sides are finalizing a $90 million purchase of structural steel and building materials Fermi had already secured. No definitive long-term lease has been signed; the company said the customer is committing capital ahead of a lease to secure power within its targeted timeline.

Fermi said it plans to mobilize on site by December 1 and targets initial power in late second quarter or early third quarter of 2027.

FRMI's Tough Road

FRMI shares have dived from their post-IPO peak amid financing concerns and the collapse of earlier tenant talks, including with Amazon and Oracle. Founder Neugebauer was ousted in April after allegations that his conduct damaged customer relations. Fermi still needs to secure project financing and satisfy conditions on its 99-year land lease with Texas Tech University by year-end, while its air permits face court challenges.
